parts.title: My life as a school radio presenter
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
I joined our school radio station two years ago, after my friend Hana told me that they needed a new presenter. I had never spoken into a microphone before, and the first time I went on air, my voice sounded so high that I wanted to hide under the table.

Now I present a programme every Tuesday at lunchtime. It lasts thirty minutes, and I play music, read the news and interview students. The part I enjoy most is the interviews, because people always say surprising things. Last month I talked to our head teacher, who told me that she used to play in a rock band.

Preparing the programme takes a lot of time. I write a plan, choose the songs and practise reading the news aloud. My teacher says that I should speak more slowly, so I put a note in front of me which says, "Slow down!"

Many people think that radio is old-fashioned, but I disagree. In my school, nearly half of the students listen every week. After I leave school, I would like to work for a real radio station.

parts.title: The story of radio
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Radio is more than a hundred years old. [1] Before that, news travelled slowly, by letter or newspaper.

In the 1920s, the first radio stations started to broadcast music and news. [2] Families gathered around a big wooden box in the evening to listen together.

During the Second World War, radio became even more important. [3] People in many countries listened to the news for hours each day, to find out what was happening.

In the 1960s, small radios with batteries appeared. [4] Young people could now listen to music wherever they were, on the beach or in the park.

Today, many people listen online or through podcasts. [5] This means that anyone with a microphone and a computer can share their ideas with the world.
sentences: Television arrived in many homes in the 1950s.
Suddenly, a voice could travel through the air for many kilometres.
She listened to it every night after dinner.
Some old radios are now worth a lot of money.
Soon, most homes in towns had a radio.
It was often the only way to hear important news.
Making programmes has also become much cheaper.
They were light enough to carry in a pocket.

gaps.explanation: A voice could travel through the air; the next sentence says that before that, news travelled slowly.
Most homes had a radio; the next sentence says families gathered around the box.
Radio was the only way to hear important news; the next sentence says people listened for hours.
The small radios were light; the next sentence says young people could listen anywhere.
Programmes are cheaper; "this means" in the next sentence says anyone can share ideas.

parts.title: A message about a new podcast
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Hi Wynn, I am writing to tell you about my new podcast. I started it [1] my brother last month. Every week, we choose a different topic and talk about it for twenty minutes. Our first programme was about school food, and it was much [2] popular than we had expected. My brother wants to [3] a famous chef to our next episode, but I do not think he will agree. [4] we record each programme, we write down a few ideas, but we never read a script. Please [5] to it and tell me what you think. I would [6] glad to hear your opinion. Cass

questions.prompt: Gap 2

questions.prompt: Gap 3

parts.title: How to start a podcast
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Starting a podcast is easier [1] you might think. First, you need an idea. Choose a subject [2] interests you, and which you are happy to talk about for hours. Next, you need some equipment. A good microphone is [3] most important thing, because poor sound makes people stop listening. You can record on your phone [4] you do not have a laptop. Choose [5] name that is short and easy to remember. Finally, tell your friends about it, and ask them [6] share it online.

gaps.explanation: Easier than you might think is a comparison.
A relative pronoun for a thing: a subject that interests you.
A superlative needs the: the most important thing.
The condition: if you have no laptop, use your phone.
Choose a name: a singular countable noun.
Ask someone to do something: ask them to share it.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Hello, listeners, this is Radio Bay with a quick change to tonight’s programme. Our teen music show, Teen Beat, used to start at six, but not this week. Tonight, the news is at six, and straight after it we have a full hour of football talk, because of the big match. Teen Beat comes after that, with seven new songs in its first hour, so please don’t switch off. And do stay with us, because at eight o’clock we have the Friday quiz, with a prize of fifty pounds. If you want to take part, send us a text during the show. Enjoy the evening, everyone!

question.explanation: Six is the old time and eight is the quiz; Teen Beat comes after the news and an hour of football talk, so it starts at seven.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Why can’t you hear the music, Mia? Is the phone out of battery?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: No, it’s at eighty per cent. I charged it all night. And the radio app is on, I checked.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Try the volume.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: It’s up. Wait, I’ve found it. One side of the headphones is cut, near the wire. My dog chewed it this morning!

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Oh no. Lucky it wasn’t the phone.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I’ll borrow my sister’s old ones until I buy new ones.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: There’s a cheap pair in the shop on the corner.

question.explanation: The phone has plenty of battery and the radio app is on; the problem is that the dog chewed the wire of the headphones.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Did you hear the new space podcast, Nora? Everyone’s talking about it.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Yes. I wanted to listen in bed, like always, but I fell asleep after two minutes the last time, so I waited. Our teacher played ten minutes at school on Tuesday, but I missed the beginning.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: So when did you hear it?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: On my way to my cousin’s yesterday. The journey takes an hour and the train was almost empty, so I heard the whole thing. Nobody was playing music for once.

turns.speaker: a

question.explanation: She decided not to listen in bed and missed the start in class; she heard the whole podcast during the hour-long journey on the train.

turns.speaker: a

turns.speaker: b

turns.speaker: a

turns.speaker: b

turns.speaker: b

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Are you ready for tomorrow, Dan? You’ll be on the school radio at nine.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I think so. People say I should be excited, and my mum is, but I’m not. I just want to get it over with.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Bored then? You looked bored in the rehearsal.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: No, I was tired. I couldn’t sleep, and I woke up three times last night. My hands are cold and I keep forgetting my first line.

turns.speaker: a

turns.speaker: b

question.prompt: How does the boy feel about being on the radio?
question.explanation: He is not excited and he explains that he was only tired, but his cold hands and the forgotten line show that he is nervous.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: If you are new in town, tune in to Riverside FM, ninety-six point two. Some people think we only play old songs, because their grandparents listen to us, and yes, we play a few in the afternoon. We also have the news every hour, but that takes just five minutes. What makes us different is the rest of the day: bands from our own streets, garage groups, school choirs and folk singers from the villages around. If you play music yourself, send us a recording, and maybe we’ll play it. Riverside FM: the sound of our local area.

question.explanation: Old songs are only a few in the afternoon and the news takes five minutes; most of the day is bands and singers from the town and its villages.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Thanks for lending me your radio, Jamie. I’ll use it at the weekend.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: No problem. But it’s old, so be gentle. I took the batteries out because they were leaking.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Ah, I see. Do I need to clean it? The box looks dusty.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Don’t worry about that, I did it this morning. Just remember to put the batteries in again before you switch it on, or it won’t work.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Good. And when do you want it back?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Sunday is fine. I’ll be at my grandma’s today, so there’s no rush.

question.explanation: He has already cleaned it and Sunday is fine for the return; the one thing she must do is put the batteries in again.

parts.title: A radio presenter's morning show
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: presenter
turns.text: Good morning, listeners, and welcome to Morning Waves, the programme that starts your day. I’m Sandor. Today is a special show, because this radio station is twenty years old. I joined five years later, but I’ve heard so many stories from the first presenters. At first, the studio was a small room above a bakery, and the presenters smelled fresh bread all day! Our first guest this morning is Mrs Ruth Hale. She comes from the town museum, not the big one in the city, and she’s going to tell us about their new exhibition. It is all about old radios. I thought it would be about telephones, which is what the poster said last week, but the plan changed. They have more than a hundred radios from the nineteen thirties, and some of them still work! Then, after the news, it’s time for your songs. You can send your messages and requests through our website, and we’ll read the best ones on air. Please don’t phone the studio this time, because the lines are busy preparing the quiz, and don’t use the app either, because it’s down for repairs. Now, the competition. Last year the prize was cinema tickets, but today a lucky winner will get two tickets for a concert next month. Just answer a question about radio history at ten o’clock. Finally, I’d like you to meet our new mascot, a hedgehog. We first called him Bubbles, but a young listener sent in a better name, so now he’s Spike. You can buy a small Spike toy at the station shop on Saturdays. He is a very popular little animal, and we hope that he will make our children’s hour even more fun. Stay with us, because we have a lot of music coming up!

gaps.prompt: Morning Waves is on a station that began ___ years ago
gaps.explanation: The station is twenty years old; Sandor joined five years later.

gaps.prompt: The first guest works at the ___ museum
gaps.explanation: She comes from the town museum, not the big one in the city.

gaps.prompt: The museum's new exhibition is about ___ from the past
gaps.explanation: The exhibition is about old radios; telephones were the first plan.

gaps.prompt: Listeners should send their song requests through the station's ___
gaps.explanation: They should use the website, not the phone or the app.

gaps.prompt: The winner of the competition will get two tickets to a ___
gaps.explanation: The prize is two tickets for a concert; cinema tickets were last year’s prize.
A listener suggested Spike; Bubbles was the first name.

parts.title: An interview with a radio presenter
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Cass, your show starts at six. What time do you get to the studio?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: My alarm goes off at four, but I live close, so I don’t leave until a quarter to five. I get in at five, make a strong coffee, and read the news. Some people think I come at six because that’s when the red light goes on, but no, I need an hour to prepare.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What’s the best thing about the job?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I get this question a lot. Choosing the music is fun, and I’ve met some singers, which was exciting at first. But now what I enjoy most is speaking to listeners, the people who call at seven in the morning. A woman once told me that I was the first voice she heard each day, and that made me feel important.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Is there anything you don’t like?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Silence. When you’re live and the computer stops, those few seconds seem like an hour, and your heart beats so fast. I don’t mind early mornings now, and I don’t write reports because there’s a team for that. But a gap on the air still scares me, and I dream about it sometimes. My colleagues laugh at me, and then they tell me about their own worst moments.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How did you get your first job?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I didn’t go to a famous school, just a small college. I did enter a competition for young presenters, but I came last! In the end, I recorded myself reading local news and sent the recordings to about twenty stations. Only one called me back, and I started the next month.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What advice would you give to people who want to do this?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Record yourself, every day, and listen to it. It’s horrible at first, but you’ll hear the mistakes. You don’t need to sing well, and you don’t need years of study. Honestly, a phone and some patience are enough. I started in my bedroom with a cheap phone, and my cat was my only audience for months, but she never complained.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: And what’s your dream for the future?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I’d love to read a children’s story on the radio, a bedtime story, with different voices for the animals. I don’t want to move to television, because I’m shy about my face, and a bookshop would be a nice hobby, but I’d have no time. The story is my real wish. I even have a favourite book ready, and I practise reading it to my nephews at weekends.
